slides.notes: Alright, moving ahead, let’s take a look at the agenda for today’s session. We’ll explore the Nano editor, learn to compress and uncompress files using tar, zip, and unzip, and practice filtering and redirection with commands like head, tail, grep, >, and piping. By the end, you’ll be able to edit, filter, and organize files right from the command line.

slides.title: Using Command line Text Editor
slides.notes: Now let's explore command line text editors

slides.title: Nano Editor
slides.body:
Text Editor
A text editor is used for editing text files.
Various text editors are:
Notepad++
Sublime Text
gEdit
Visual Studio Code 
   etc..
slides.notes:
Let's talk about text editors before we dive into Nano.
Text editors are specialized programs for creating and modifying text files.
You're probably familiar with some graphical editors like Notepad++, Sublime Text, gEdit, and Visual Studio Code.
In the command line, we have similar tools but with text-based interfaces.
These editors are essential for programming, configuring systems, and working with text files.

slides.title: Nano Editor
slides.body:
Nano
Nano is an easy to use command line text editor for Unix and Linux-based operating systems
GNU nano 4.8                      practice 
^G Get Help  ^O Write Out   ^W Where Is  ^K Cut Text     ^J Justify    ^C Cur Pos
^X Exit      ^R Read File   ^\ Replace   ^U Paste Text   ^T To Spell   ^_ Go To Line
Editor
slides.notes:
Now let's look at Nano, a beginner-friendly command line text editor.
Nano is designed to be simple and intuitive for Unix and Linux systems.
On screen, we can see the Nano interface with a file called "practice" open.
Notice the commands at the bottom - these are your control keys. The ^ symbol means "Ctrl".
For example, Ctrl+G gets help, Ctrl+O saves your file, and Ctrl+X exits.
Nano is perfect for beginners because it displays these commands right on screen, unlike some other text editors.

slides.title: Nano Editor
slides.body:
Open File
To open a file with nano,
pass the filename as an argument
$ nano filepath
Syntax
$ nano practice.txt
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  nano.
slides.notes:
Let's learn how to open a file with Nano.
The syntax is simple - just type "nano" followed by the filename.
In our example, "nano practice.txt" opens the file practice.txt for editing.
If the file doesn't exist yet, Nano will create it when you save.
This is your first Nano command - opening or creating a file.

slides.title: Editing Files
slides.body:
Updating File
GNU nano 4.8                      practice 
Hello World!
^G Get Help  ^O Write Out   ^W Where Is  ^K Cut Text     ^J Justify    ^C Cur Pos
^X Exit      ^R Read File   ^\ Replace   ^U Paste Text   ^T To Spell   ^_ Go To Line
Add the text of the file in the middle of the editor
Editor
Commands we have learned so far:  nano.
slides.notes:
Once Nano is open, editing is straightforward.
Simply type your text in the middle section of the editor. Here, some text is there i.e "Hello World!".
You can use your arrow keys to navigate the file and make changes wherever needed.
Nano works much like any text editor, except it's all in the terminal.
The commands at the bottom remain visible to help you with common actions.

slides.title: Editing Files
slides.body:
Saving File
To save a file, press Ctrl+O and Enter()
Commands we have learned so far:  nano.    
GNU nano 4.8                      practice 
Hello World!
                           [ Wrote 1 line ]
^G Get Help  ^O Write Out   ^W Where Is  ^K Cut Text     ^J Justify    ^C Cur Pos
^X Exit      ^R Read File   ^\ Replace   ^U Paste Text   ^T To Spell   ^_ Go To Line
Editor
slides.notes:
‘O’ save your file in Nano, press Ctrl+O (that's the letter O, not zero).
After pressing Ctrl+O, Nano will ask you to confirm the filename. Just press Enter to accept.
Notice the confirmation message "Wrote 1 line" indicating our file was saved successfully.
This is much like using "Save" in graphical editors, but with keyboard shortcuts.
Remember: Ctrl+O to save (Write Out) is one of the most important Nano commands.

slides.title: Editing Files
slides.body:
Exit Nano
To exit from nano editor, press Ctrl+X
Commands we have learned so far:  nano.    
GNU nano 4.8                      practice 
Hello World!
^G Get Help  ^O Write Out   ^W Where Is  ^K Cut Text     ^J Justify    ^C Cur Pos
^X Exit      ^R Read File   ^\ Replace   ^U Paste Text   ^T To Spell   ^_ Go To Line
Editor
slides.notes:
To exit Nano, simply press Ctrl+X.
If you've made changes since your last save, Nano will ask if you want to save them before exiting.

The basic workflow is: open a file, make your changes, save with Ctrl+O, and exit with Ctrl+X.

slides.title: Editing Files
slides.body:
Viewing File Contents
Commands we have learned so far:  nano.    
$ cat practice.txt
Hello World!
Bash
slides.notes:
After exiting Nano, let's verify our file was saved properly.
We can use the "cat" command we learned earlier to display the file contents.
In our example, "cat practice.txt" shows "Hello World!" - exactly what we typed in Nano.
This confirms our file was created and saved successfully.
Remember that cat is great for quick viewing, while Nano is for editing.

slides.title: Filtering & Output Redirection
slides.notes: Now we're moving to an important topic: filtering and output redirection.

slides.title: Editing Files
slides.body:
Filtering
We can filter the contents of a file using the following filter commands.
head
tail
grep
slides.notes:
Let's explore three essential filtering commands for working with file contents.
First is "head", which shows the beginning of a file.
Second is "tail", which displays the end of a file.
Third is "grep", which searches for specific patterns or text within files.
These commands help you quickly find what you need in large files without opening the entire file for editing.

slides.title: Filtering
slides.body:
Head
Used to print top N lines of a file
By default, it will print the first 10 lines 
$ head -2 sentences.txt
There was a heavy dew this morning
Do Meditation, yoga and exercise
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  head.    
head [-N] filename
Syntax
slides.notes:
The "head" command shows the beginning of a file.
By default, head displays the first 10 lines, but you can specify any number with the -N option.
In our example, "head -2 sentences.txt" shows just the first two lines of the file: "There was a heavy dew this morning" and "Do Meditation, yoga and exercise".
This is useful when you need to quickly check what's at the beginning of a large file without loading the entire content.

slides.title: Filtering
slides.body:
Tail
Used to print last N lines of a file
By default it will print the last 10 lines 
$ tail -2 sentences.txt
This morning was no exception
The morning after came without shame or embarrassment
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  head. .tail.     
tail [-N] filename
Syntax
slides.notes:
The "tail" command is essentially the opposite of head - it shows the end of a file.
By default, tail displays the last 10 lines, but like head, you can specify a number with -N.
In our example, "tail -2 sentences.txt" shows the last two lines of the file.
This is particularly useful for checking log files where the newest information is often at the end.

slides.title: Counting
slides.body:
Word Count
wc is used to find out number of lines, word count and characters count in the files 
wc filename
Syntax
$ wc sentences.txt
18   102  594 sentences.txt
Bash
line count
word count
character count
Commands we have learned so far:  head. .tail..wc.
slides.notes:
The "wc" command (short for "word count") gives you statistics about a file.
It displays three numbers: line count, word count, and character count.
In our example, "wc sentences.txt" shows:
18 lines
102 words
594 characters
This is helpful for quickly analyzing text files without reading them completely.
You can also use options like wc -l for just line count, wc -w for word count, or wc -c for character count.

slides.title: Piping
slides.body:
Using ‘|’
Pipe is used to combine two or more commands
Output of one command is passed as an input to the command followed and so on.
command 1 | command_2 |command N
Syntax
$ cat sentences.txt | head -2 
There was a heavy dew this morning
Do Meditation, yoga and exercise
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  head. .tail...wc...|.
slides.notes:
Now let's learn about the pipe symbol (|) - one of the most powerful features of the command line.
Piping connects commands by sending the output of one command as input to another.
In our example, "cat sentences.txt | head -2" first reads the file with cat, then pipes that output to head -2, which shows only the first two lines.
This is like creating a production line where each command performs its task on the data.
You can chain multiple commands together for complex operations.
The pipe is essential for building efficient command line workflows.

slides.title: Filtering
slides.body:
Grep
Searches a file or files for lines that have a certain pattern
$ cat sentences.txt | grep "morning"
There was a heavy dew this morning
There was a heavy dew this morning
This morning was no exception
The morning after came without shame or embarrassment
...
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  head. .tail...grep...wc...|.
cat filename | grep pattern
Syntax
slides.notes:
The "grep" command is a powerful search tool that finds patterns in text.
Combined with piping, it lets you filter for specific content in files.
In our example, "cat sentences.txt | grep "morning"" shows only lines containing the word "morning".
Notice how it found four matching lines from our file.
Grep is case-sensitive by default, so "Morning" and "morning" would be treated differently.
This is incredibly useful for finding specific information in large files.

slides.title: Piping
slides.body:
Example 1
$ cat sentences.txt | grep "morning" | wc  
12  81 462
Bash
line count
Commands we have learned so far:  head. .tail...grep...wc...|.
Number of lines that contain the word morning in the given file
slides.notes:
Here's a great example of combining multiple commands with pipes.
The command "cat sentences.txt | grep "morning" | wc" does the following:
cat reads the file
grep filters for lines containing "morning"
wc counts the results
We can see there are 12 lines containing "morning" in our file.
This powerful combination lets you extract specific information and analyze it in one command.

slides.title: Output Redirection
slides.body:
Operator : ">"
">" takes the standard output of the command and redirects it to the file
command > filename
Syntax
$ cat sentences.txt | head -2 > learnings.txt
$ cat learnings.txt
There was a heavy dew this morning
Do Meditation, yoga and exercise
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  head. .tail...grep...wc...|...>.
slides.notes:
Now let's learn about the ">" redirection operator.
This symbol captures the output of a command and saves it to a file instead of displaying it on screen.
In our example, "cat sentences.txt | head -2 > learnings.txt" takes the first two lines and saves them to a new file called learnings.txt.
When we check with "cat learnings.txt", we see those two lines were saved.
Important: If the target file already exists, ">" will overwrite it completely.
This is useful for saving command results for later use.

slides.title: Compressing & Decompressing Files
slides.notes: Moving on , let’s understand Compressing and Decompressing Files

slides.title: Working with Files
slides.body:
Compressing & Decompressing Files
1
File compression is a reduction in the number of bits needed to store the data of a file.
2
Files are stored in such a way that, it uses less disk space than all the individual files and directories combined
slides.notes:
Now let's explore file compression, a technique that helps save storage space.
Compression reduces the number of bits needed to store data, making files smaller.
There are two key benefits:
Compressed files use less disk space
Compressed files transfer faster between devices or over networks
Linux provides several tools for compressing and Decompressing files.

slides.title: Working with Files
slides.body:
Compressing & Decompressing Files
index.html
video.mp4
compressed.zip
...
...
folder
Compressing
Decompressing / Extraction
Advantages of compressing files are:
1
taking less disk space
2
easier and faster transmission
slides.notes:
Compression offers two major advantages:
First, compressed files take up less disk space, which is important when storage is limited.
Second, smaller files transfer faster over networks or between devices.
The diagram shows how multiple files like index.html, video.mp4, and folders can be compressed into a single zip file.
Later, this compressed file can be Decompressed or extracted back to its original components.

slides.title: Working with Files
slides.body:
Compressing & Decompressing Files
index.html
video.mp4
compressed.zip
...
...
folder
Compressing
Decompressing / Extraction
Commonly used file formats for the compressed files:
gzip
zip
tar
slides.notes:
Linux supports several compression formats, each with different commands:
First is "gzip" - a popular compression format in Linux systems.
Second is "zip" - widely used across different operating systems, making it good for sharing files.
Third is "tar" - technically an archiving tool, but it's often combined with compression.
Each format has specific commands for compressing and extracting files.

slides.title: Compressing/Decompressing Files
slides.body:
tar
.
├── report.txt
└── videos
    └── conf-video.mp4
Current Working Directory
slides.notes:
Let's look at using tar for compression.
Here we have our current working directory with two files: a small text file called report.txt (270 bytes) and a much larger video file called conf-video.mp4 (58 megabytes).
The directory structure shows report.txt at the top level and conf-video.mp4 in a videos subdirectory.
Tar is especially useful for preserving this directory structure while compressing multiple files into a single archive.

slides.title: Compressing/Decompressing Files
slides.body:
tar
We can use tar to compress files & directories
Syntax
tar -czvf file-name.tar.gz path1 path2 ..
$ tar -czvf my_collection.tar.gz videos report.txt
videos/
videos/conf-video.mp4
report.txt
$ ls
my_collection.tar.gz  report.txt  videos
Bash
slides.notes:
To compress files with tar, we use the command "tar -czvf" followed by the archive name and files to include.
The options mean:
c: create a new archive
z: compress with gzip
v: verbose (show progress)
f: specify the filename
In our example, "tar -czvf my_collection.tar.gz videos report.txt" compresses both the videos directory and report.txt file.
The output shows each file being added to the archive.
When we check with ls, we see our new compressed file alongside the originals.

slides.title: Compressing/Decompressing Files
slides.body:
tar
Commands we have learned so far:  .tar. 
.
├── my_collection.tar.gz
├── report.txt
└── videos
    └── conf-video.mp4
Current Working Directory
slides.notes:
Alright, let's look at the results of our compression.
Our current directory now contains three items: the original report.txt file, the videos directory with conf-video.mp4, and our new compressed archive my_collection.tar.gz.
Looking at the file sizes, we can see:
report.txt is 270 bytes
conf-video.mp4 is 58M
my_collection.tar.gz is 57M
Notice the compressed archive is only slightly smaller than the video file alone. This is because video files are already compressed, so tar can't reduce their size much further.
Text files compress much better than media files.

slides.title: Compressing/Decompressing Files
slides.body:
Extract
Syntax
tar -xzvf  filename.tar.gz -C path
$ mkdir collections
$ tar -xzvf my_collection.tar.gz -C collections
videos/
videos/conf-video.mp4
report.txt
$ cd collections
$ ls
report.txt  videos
Commands we have learned so far:  .tar. 
Bash
slides.notes:
Next, let's learn how to extract our tar archive.
To extract, we use "tar -xzvf" followed by the archive name, and optionally "-C" to specify a destination directory.
The options mean:
x: extract
z: decompress from gzip
v: verbose (show progress)
f: specify the filename
In our example, we first create a new directory called "collections". Then we extract my_collection.tar.gz into this directory using "tar -xzvf my_collection.tar.gz -C collections".
Moving to the collections directory, we can see that all files were extracted with their original structure intact.

slides.title: Compressing/Decompressing Files
slides.body:
tar
.
├── collections
│   ├── report.txt
│   └── videos
│       └── conf-video.mp4
...
Current Working Directory
Commands we have learned so far:  .tar.
slides.notes:
Moving on, let's see what our directory structure looks like after extraction.
Our current working directory now contains a "collections" folder, which has the exact same structure as what we compressed:
report.txt at the top level
A videos folder containing conf-video.mp4
This demonstrates one of tar's key features - it preserves the original directory structure when extracting.
This is particularly useful when sharing complex projects with multiple folders and files.

slides.title: Compressing/Decompressing Files
slides.body:
zip
It is used to package all the files into one file with .zip extension
zip -r zipfile.zip file1 folder1 file2 ...
Syntax
$ ls
report.txt        videos          
$ zip -r collections.zip videos report.txt
  adding: videos/ (stored 0%)
  adding: videos/conf-video.mp4 (deflated 3%)
  adding: report.txt (deflated 39%)
Bash
Note: zip uses bzip2 file format by default
Commands we have learned so far:  tar. zip.
slides.notes:
Alright, now let's learn about the zip command, which creates archives with the familiar .zip extension.
Unlike tar, which is mainly used in Linux, zip files are recognized across all operating systems, making them ideal for sharing files.
The syntax is "zip -r zipfile.zip file1 folder1..." where the -r option means include subdirectories recursively.
In our example, "zip -r collections.zip videos report.txt" packages both items into collections.zip.
Notice the output shows different compression rates - the text file was reduced by 39% while the video was only reduced by 3%, again showing that text compresses much better than media.

slides.title: Compressing/Decompressing Files
slides.body:
unzip
The unzip command extracts all files from the specified ZIP archive 
unzip filename.zip -d path 
Syntax
$ mkdir new-folder
$ unzip collections.zip -d new-folder
Archive:  collections.zip
   creating: new-folder/videos/
  inflating: new-folder/videos/conf-video.mp4  
  inflating: new-folder/report.txt          
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  tar. .zip.  unzip.
slides.notes:
Moving forward, let's learn how to extract zip files using the unzip command.
The syntax is "unzip filename.zip -d destination" where -d specifies where to extract the files.
In our example, we first create a directory called "new-folder". Then we extract collections.zip into this directory with "unzip collections.zip -d new-folder".
The output shows each file being "inflated" or extracted to its proper location.
This process works similarly to tar extraction but uses different commands specific to the zip format.

Key Takeaways
slides.notes:
Finally, let's recap what we learned in today’s session.
We learned to edit files with Nano using simple keyboard shortcuts.
We explored filtering with head, tail, and grep for finding specific content.
We used piping (|) to connect commands and redirection (>) to save output.
And we covered file compression with tar and zip/unzip for efficient storage and sharing.
These tools complete your essential file management toolkit in Linux.

An important point you always need to remember: 

PRACTICE. PRACTICE. PRACTICE. 

The more you practice, the better you will get at working with various question formats.
